title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXVI
paragraphs:
’Tis one thing to be tempted, Escalus,
Another thing to fall.
—_Measure for Measure_.

Lydgate had good reason to value the way his practice relieved his private anxieties. He no longer had enough spare energy for independent research or speculative thought. But at a patient’s bedside, immediate demands on his judgment and sympathy gave him the extra force needed to draw him out of himself. This was more than the helpful harness of routine that lets foolish men live respectably and unhappy men live calmly. It continually required fresh thought and attention to another person’s needs and suffering. Looking back over our lives, many of us would say that the kindest man we have known was a doctor. Perhaps he was the surgeon whose delicate tact, guided by deep understanding, brought help in our hour of need more sublime than any miracle worker’s. Some of that mercy, blessing both giver and receiver, always accompanied Lydgate at the Hospital and in his patients’ homes. Better than any opiate, it soothed and sustained him through his anxieties and his sense that his mind was deteriorating.

Mr. Farebrother’s suspicion about opium had nevertheless been correct. When approaching difficulties first began to chafe, and when Lydgate first realized what his marriage would require if it were not to become loneliness in harness—the effort to keep loving without caring too much about being loved—he had tried a dose once or twice. But he had no inherited physical craving for such brief escapes from haunting misery. He was strong and could drink plenty of wine, but felt no desire for it. When other men drank spirits, he took sugar and water, looking with contemptuous pity even on the earliest excitement caused by alcohol. Gambling affected him similarly. He had watched plenty in Paris, observing it as one might a disease. Winning money tempted him no more than drink. He had told himself that the only kind of success worth having must come through a conscious process of difficult, elevated reasoning directed toward a useful result. The power he wanted could never be represented by trembling fingers grasping a pile of coins, or the half-savage, half-idiotic triumph in the eyes of a man sweeping up the stakes of twenty crestfallen companions.

Yet, as he had tried opium, he now began thinking about gambling. He did not hunger for its excitement. Rather, he cast a wistful inward glance at an easy way of obtaining money that required no begging and created no obligations. Had he been in London or Paris, those thoughts, helped by opportunity, would probably have taken him into a gambling house. This time he would not have watched the gamblers, but watched alongside them with the same eagerness. His immense need to win, if chance would only allow it, would have overcome his disgust. An incident not long after the collapse of his airy hopes of help from his uncle showed strongly what a real opportunity to gamble might have produced.

A particular set of men frequented the Green Dragon’s billiard room. Most, like our acquaintance Mr. Bambridge, were known as men of pleasure. Here poor Fred Vincy had incurred part of his memorable debt, losing bets and having to borrow from that merry companion. Middlemarch generally knew that substantial sums changed hands there. The Green Dragon’s resulting reputation for dissipation naturally made it more tempting in some quarters. Like initiates of Freemasonry, its regulars probably wished they had something more tremendous to keep secret. But they were not a closed society. Plenty of respectable men, old and young, occasionally entered the billiard room to see what was happening. Lydgate had the physical skill for billiards and enjoyed the game. Soon after coming to Middlemarch he had once or twice taken a turn with the cue at the Green Dragon. Later he had neither time to play nor any desire for its company. One evening, however, he had reason to look for Mr. Bambridge there. The horse dealer had promised to find a buyer for his remaining good horse. Lydgate had decided to replace it with a cheap hack, hoping the reduction in style might bring him twenty pounds. Every small sum now mattered as a way of keeping his tradesmen patient. Stopping upstairs in the billiard room as he passed would save time.

Mr. Bambridge had not arrived, his friend Mr. Horrock said, but was sure to come later. Lydgate stayed and played a game to fill the time. That evening his eyes had the peculiar brightness and his manner the unusual animation Mr. Farebrother had once noticed. His unexpected appearance attracted plenty of attention among the Middlemarch company. Several spectators, as well as players, were betting eagerly. Lydgate played well and felt confident. Bets fell around him, and a quick thought came that his winnings might double the amount he would save on the horse. He began backing his own shots and won repeatedly. Mr. Bambridge arrived without his noticing. Beyond the excitement of play, he was seeing visions of going to Brassing the next day, where gambling took place on a larger scale. Perhaps one powerful snatch at the devil’s bait could tear it free of the hook and buy release from his daily demands for payment.

He was still winning when two more visitors entered. One was young Hawley, newly returned from his law studies in London; the other was Fred Vincy, who had lately spent several evenings at his old haunt. Hawley was a skilled billiard player and brought a cool, fresh hand to the cue. Fred, startled to find Lydgate there and astonished at his excited betting, stood back outside the circle around the table.

Recently Fred had been rewarding determination with a little indulgence. For six months he had worked willingly at every kind of outdoor task under Mr. Garth. Through rigorous practice he had almost corrected his bad handwriting, though the practice was perhaps less rigorous because he often did it in the evenings at Mr. Garth’s house under Mary’s eyes. During the past fortnight, however, Mary had been staying with the ladies at Lowick Parsonage while Mr. Farebrother stayed in Middlemarch carrying out parish plans. Finding nothing more pleasant to do, Fred had gone to the Green Dragon, partly for billiards and partly to savor the old talk about horses, sport, and life viewed from an angle that was not rigorously proper. He had not hunted once that season, owned no riding horse, and had traveled mostly in Mr. Garth’s gig or on the steady cob Mr. Garth could lend him. It seemed a little hard, Fred began to think, to be kept more strictly in harness than a clergyman. “I’ll tell you something, Mistress Mary: learning surveying and drawing plans will be harder than writing sermons,” he had said, wanting her to appreciate his sacrifices. “Hercules and Theseus were nothing compared with me. They had sport and never learned a bookkeeper’s hand.” Now that Mary was away briefly, Fred had made a small escape, like a strong dog that cannot slip its collar and pulls the chain’s staple out instead. Naturally he meant to go neither fast nor far. There was no reason not to play billiards, but he was determined not to bet. His present financial ambition was heroic: to save almost all the eighty pounds Mr. Garth offered him and give it back. He could easily do this by abandoning useless spending, since he had more clothes than he needed and paid nothing for his board. Within a year he could repay much of the ninety pounds he had cost Mrs. Garth, unfortunately at a time when she needed it more than now. Nevertheless, on this evening, his fifth recent visit, ten pounds occupied his mind, though it was not in his pocket. It was the amount he intended to keep from his half-year’s salary, with the pleasure ahead of taking thirty pounds to Mrs. Garth when Mary would probably be home. He thought of that ten pounds as a fund from which he might risk a little if a promising bet arose. Why not? When sovereigns were flying about, why shouldn’t he catch a few? He would never go far down that road again. Still, a man likes to assure himself and his pleasure-loving fellows how much mischief he could do if he chose. If he refrains from making himself ill, ruining himself, or talking as loosely as human limitations allow, it is not because he is a simpleton. Fred did not formulate reasons. Formal reasoning represents very imperfectly the tingling return of old habits and the whims of young blood. But that evening he carried a lurking expectation that once he played he would begin to bet, enjoy a little punch, and generally arrange to feel “rather seedy” the next morning. Actions often begin in such undefined movements.

Almost the last thing Fred expected was to see his brother-in-law looking excited and placing bets just as he himself might. He had never entirely abandoned his old opinion that Lydgate was a prig, overwhelmingly conscious of his superiority. The sight shocked Fred more than his vague knowledge of Lydgate’s debts and his father’s refusal to help could fully explain. His own desire to join the game abruptly stopped. Their positions had strangely reversed. Fred’s fair face and blue eyes, usually bright, careless, and ready for any promise of amusement, had grown involuntarily serious and almost embarrassed, as if at something improper. Meanwhile Lydgate, normally so composed and strong, with an underlying thoughtfulness behind even his sharpest attention, now acted, watched, and spoke with the excited, narrowed awareness of a creature with fierce eyes and retractable claws.

By betting on his own shots, Lydgate had won sixteen pounds. Young Hawley’s arrival changed the balance. Hawley made excellent shots himself and began betting against Lydgate’s. Lydgate’s nervous strain shifted from confidence in his own skill to defiance of another man’s doubt. Defiance excited him more, but gave him less certainty. He continued backing himself and began missing frequently. Still he played on. His mind was as completely confined within the steep-sided crevice of the game as that of the idlest ignoramus present. Fred saw him losing rapidly and found himself in the unfamiliar position of racking his brains for a way to interrupt without giving offense, perhaps providing an excuse to leave. Others, he noticed, were also watching Lydgate’s strange departure from his usual self. A touch on the elbow and a request for a private word might wake him from his absorption. Fred could think of nothing cleverer than the boldly unlikely claim that he wanted to visit Rosy and wondered whether she was home that evening. He was about to try this desperate, flimsy device when a waiter brought word that Mr. Farebrother was downstairs and wanted to speak to him.
Surprised and somewhat uneasy, Fred sent word that he would come at once. With a fresh impulse he went to Lydgate, asked, “Could I have a word?” and drew him aside.
“Farebrother has sent up to say he wants me. He’s downstairs. I thought you might want to know, in case you had something to say to him.”

Fred had seized this excuse simply because he could not say, “You’re losing horribly and everyone is staring. You’d better leave.” Yet inspiration could scarcely have served him better. Lydgate had not noticed Fred. His sudden appearance, announcing Mr. Farebrother, struck like a sharp blow.
“No, no,” Lydgate said. “I’ve nothing particular to tell him. But the game’s over. I must leave. I only came to find Bambridge.”
“He’s over there, making a noise. I don’t think he’s ready for business. Come down to Farebrother with me. I expect I’m in for a scolding, and you can protect me,” Fred added with some skill.

Lydgate felt ashamed, but could not bear to reveal it by refusing to see Mr. Farebrother. He went downstairs. They merely shook hands and spoke about the frost. Once the three reached the street, the Vicar seemed quite ready to say goodbye to Lydgate. He clearly wanted to speak to Fred alone. “I interrupted you, young gentleman, because I’ve urgent business with you,” he said kindly. “Will you walk with me to St. Botolph’s?”
It was a fine night, thick with stars. Mr. Farebrother suggested taking a longer route to the old church by the London road. His next words were—
“I thought Lydgate never visited the Green Dragon.”
“So did I,” Fred said. “He told me he’d come to see Bambridge.”
“Then he wasn’t playing?”
Fred had not intended to disclose this, but now had to answer, “Yes, he was. I suppose it was just by chance. I’ve never seen him there before.”
“So you’ve been going often yourself lately?”
“Oh, five or six times.”
“I believe you had a good reason for giving up those visits?”
“Yes. You know the whole story,” said Fred, disliking this catechism. “I told you everything.”

“Which I suppose gives me some right to raise it now. We understand each other, don’t we? We’re friends who can speak openly. I’ve listened to you, and you’ll be willing to listen to me. May I take a turn at talking about myself?”
“I’m deeply in your debt, Mr. Farebrother,” Fred said, full of uncomfortable guesses.

“I won’t pretend you owe me nothing. But I must confess, Fred, that just now I was tempted to undo all that by keeping quiet. Someone told me, ‘Young Vincy is back at the billiard table every night. He won’t stand restraint for long.’ I felt tempted to do the opposite of what I’m doing: say nothing and wait for you to climb back down the ladder, first betting, then—”
“I haven’t bet anything,” Fred interrupted quickly.

“I’m glad. But my impulse was to watch you take the wrong turn, exhaust Garth’s patience, and lose the best chance of your life, the chance you worked rather hard to secure. You can guess what feeling tempted me. I’m sure you know. I’m sure you understand that fulfilling your affections stands in the way of fulfilling mine.”
He paused, apparently waiting for acknowledgment. The feeling audible in his fine voice gave his words solemn weight. But no other emotion could overcome Fred’s alarm.
“You couldn’t expect me to give her up,” he said after a moment. This was no occasion for pretending generosity.

“Certainly not, when she returned your love. But relationships like these, however long they have lasted, can always change. I can easily imagine your behaving in a way that weakens her attachment. Remember, her commitment to you is conditional. Another man, who perhaps believes he has some claim on her regard, might then win the secure place in her love as well as her respect that you had allowed to slip away. I can quite easily imagine that outcome,” Mr. Farebrother repeated emphatically. “A companionship of ready sympathy can outweigh even the longest shared history.” Fred felt that a beak and talons could hardly have made the Vicar’s attack crueler than his capable tongue did. A horrible conviction seized him that behind these hypothetical statements lay knowledge of an actual change in Mary’s feelings.

“Of course I know it could easily be over for me,” Fred said in distress. “If she’s started comparing—” He stopped, unwilling to expose everything he felt, then added with a little bitterness to help him, “But I thought you were my friend.”

“I am. That’s why we’re here. But I’ve felt a strong inclination not to be. I’ve told myself, ‘If that youngster is likely to harm his own prospects, why interfere? Aren’t you worth as much as he is? Don’t those extra sixteen years of yours, in which you’ve gone rather hungry, give you more right to satisfaction? If there’s a chance he’ll go to the dogs, let him. Perhaps you couldn’t stop him anyway. Take the benefit yourself.’”

During the pause that followed, a deeply unpleasant chill seized Fred. What came next? He dreaded hearing that something had been said to Mary. This felt more like a threat than a warning. When Farebrother spoke again, however, his tone changed with the encouragement of music moving into a major key.

“But once I intended something better, and I’ve returned to that intention. I thought, Fred, that hardly anything could help me _hold to it_ better than telling you exactly what I’ve been feeling. Do you understand me now? I want you to make her life happy, and your own. If there’s any chance a warning from me might prevent something that would endanger that, well, I’ve given it.”

The Vicar’s voice dropped at the end. They stood on a patch of grass where the road branched toward St. Botolph’s. He paused and held out his hand, as if closing the conversation. Fred felt a new kind of emotion. Someone particularly responsive to a noble act has said it sends a regenerating shudder through the body and makes one ready to begin life again. Fred Vincy was experiencing a good deal of that effect.
“I’ll try to be worthy,” he said, stopping before he added, “of you as well as her.” Meanwhile, Mr. Farebrother had gathered the impulse to say more.
“Don’t imagine I believe her preference for you has weakened at present, Fred. Rest assured: if you keep on the right path, the rest will go right too.”
“I’ll never forget what you’ve done,” Fred replied. “Nothing I can say seems worth saying. Only I’ll try not to waste your kindness.”
“That’s enough. Goodbye, and God bless you.”

They parted there, but both walked for a long time before leaving the starlight. Much of Fred’s thinking could be reduced to this: “Marrying Farebrother would certainly have been a fine thing for her. But if she loves me most, and I’m a good husband?”

Perhaps Mr. Farebrother’s thoughts could be compressed into a single shrug and a few words. “What a part one little woman can play in a man’s life! Giving her up can be a very good imitation of heroism, and winning her can become a discipline.”
